description: We are a family team taking on the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.
summary:
Galaxya.Space is a dynamic game and learning platform where kids ages 7 to 12 practice engineering decisions while running a Moon base. It turns real space data into experiences they can understand, where every decision has a consequence.
The platform is designed to query NASA’s public APIs automatically every 24 hours and add new valid records to future missions. Kids see real NASA images and face challenges tied to documented events like solar activity and space weather. Their effect on the base follows simplified educational rules.
In each mission, players manage a limited battery and choose how to split power and work between research, repairs and radiation shelter. They predict, decide, observe and explain, and learn what each choice gains and costs.
Manny, a manatee astronaut created by our team and inspired by Florida’s wildlife, guides the adventure with curiosity, ingenuity and graded hints. Finishing a mission earns a certificate that recognizes the mission completed, to download or have emailed by a parent.
We turn real NASA data into game decisions that help kids understand, plan and learn. It is free, works on computers and phones, and needs no sign-up.
details:
galaxya.space is a free, browser-based educational game and dynamic learning platform for children ages 7–12. Its central purpose is to introduce children to the world of data and images produced by NASA: how observations are collected, what they represent, and how people use them to understand the universe and make decisions.

The game is the medium for that learning. Children encounter authentic scientific information, explore its meaning and see how selected data affects a mission model. Our intended impact is to help them recognize that space science is an ongoing process of observing, collecting evidence, interpreting information and testing ideas.

HOW CHILDREN LEARN

The platform connects real NASA images and records with a learning cycle:

Observe → question → predict → decide → see consequences → explain → apply the idea again.

Images are presented with their source and credit, and the date when it is known, connecting the adventure to actual observations. As the platform develops, the educational goal is to help children understand what collected the information, what it tells us and what its limitations are.

In our first playable mission, “The Shadow Window,” children manage a Moon base with limited battery power. They balance research, repairs and crew protection. Before each stage, they predict what will happen, choose an action and receive an explanation of the result.

A documented NASA solar-flare record helps select the scenario (the game uses flares older than 14 days, so their linked particle events are on record). Its classification changes a simplified educational shelter rule. We distinguish the observed event from our teaching model: the game does not calculate actual lunar radiation exposure or provide real operational guidance.

This distinction is itself part of the educational purpose. Children should learn that an observation provides evidence, while a model uses assumptions and rules to explore possible consequences.

Manny, our manatee astronaut inspired by Florida’s wildlife, offers graded hints, from a gentle nudge to a bigger clue. A guided introduction and practice activity teach the controls before the main challenge. There are no rankings or time pressure, allowing children to experiment and reflect.

THE CERTIFICATE

Completing a mission earns a Certificate of Mission Complete, issued by Galaxya.Space and signed by Manny, “your mission companion.” It carries the child's first name, the mission, the stars earned out of 15, the real solar alert that shaped the mission with its class and date, and its own certificate number. Children can download it, or an adult can have it emailed from hello@galaxya.space with the PDF attached. It recognizes mission completion, not independently verified scientific proficiency.

WHAT MAKES THE PLATFORM DYNAMIC

The platform is configured to check selected public NASA sources every 24 hours. Validated updates can refresh discovery content and shape subsequent mission scenarios. Individual sources publish at different frequencies, and newly published images may depict earlier observations.

Dynamic data provides fresh opportunities to learn. A new record is valuable when children can understand what it represents, identify what it changes in the model and explain how that affects their choices.

Each playthrough retains its starting conditions. New information can influence future missions without changing a mission already underway. Planned comparison activities will hold external conditions constant so children can explore the consequences of changing their own decisions.

Scientific updates and educational progression have separate roles: data changes the environment, while learning design determines appropriate explanations, hints and complexity.

The first lunar mission is playable. Mission Academy, additional NASA Missions, Mission Lab and My Mission Log form the broader roadmap for guided practice, changing challenges, controlled comparisons and reflection. In the long term, we hope to grow galaxya.space into a family of missions built from new NASA data, always designed for children ages 7–12.

NASA API ANALYSIS, DATA MODEL AND DATA DICTIONARY

To support this educational platform, we built a reusable foundation for retrieving, documenting and interpreting NASA information.

Our analysis covered 16 API families in the api.nasa.gov catalog and recorded 13,590 fields, including inputs, outputs and allowed values. We documented types, units, definition sources and official descriptions where available.

We mapped 7,829 fields to columns in our own database. The platform’s data dictionary documents 8,875 columns across 327 data tables and resides inside the database itself.

Definitions come from official contracts where available: the Exoplanet Archive’s TAP schema, including 5,213 columns; DONKI and TechPort OpenAPI files; the SSC schema; and JPL documentation. Fields identified from observed responses rather than formal contracts are marked as non-contractual.

For 6,757 fields, the source provides no description. The dictionary records that absence rather than inventing an explanation.

The mapped columns are classified by purpose:

• 150 for the game.

• 425 for the home page.

• 55 for source credits.

• 7,199 retained for future games and experiences.

These classifications distinguish application needs from future capacity. A stored field does not automatically influence gameplay or have an approved educational interpretation.

Core tables include space_source, space_feed, space_fetch_run, space_raw_record, space_event, space_event_link, space_observation, space_media and space_map_layer, alongside collection-specific api_* tables.

Original API records are preserved alongside structured representations, supporting traceability and future processing. An automated check identifies undocumented tables or columns; the current dictionary reports none. The complete 13,590-row field matrix is maintained in our private Gitea repository.

FROM DATA TO A LEARNING EXPERIENCE

A server-side loader retrieves NASA records, validates them and stores them in PostgreSQL. The website and game read from this local database rather than making separate NASA requests from each child’s browser. Previously loaded content remains available during source outages.

Images are stored with their source, date, credits and checksum. The architecture separates ingestion, storage, mission rules and presentation, allowing new sources to be connected without rebuilding the entire platform.

However, connecting an API is not enough. Before information affects a mission, we must establish its scientific meaning, define a defensible model relationship and identify the learning opportunity it supports.

Our governing relationship is:

Authentic observation → understandable evidence → model condition → meaningful decision → visible consequence → explanation.

The daily retrieval runs at 04:30 New York time through a scheduled task; it was activated on November 15, 2026 and its first automatic run is on November 16.

INFRASTRUCTURE AND TOOLS

Hardware: we develop, test and stage on our own local infrastructure, a rack of servers with a Synology storage server that also holds our backups. The public platform runs on a separate virtual private server. We test across 16 emulated screen sizes.

We developed our own hosting environment on a Debian 13 virtual server using PostgreSQL 18, Apache and PHP 8.5 with PHP-FPM. Each hosted site has a separate process pool, database and database role.

Cloudflare Tunnel publishes the platform without opening inbound web ports on the origin server. This environment supports scheduled retrieval, structured storage, image delivery, gameplay and certificates.

The browser experience uses HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript. Gitea and continuous integration support development, and Chromium supports automated browser testing.

Security controls include restricted SSH-key administration, service isolation, controlled outbound connections, automatic security updates, prepared database queries and credentials outside the web root. Certificate requests are validated and rate-limited.

Encrypted hourly backups are copied to separate storage, with weekly automated restore testing.

PLANNING, VALIDATION AND PRODUCTION RELEASES

The project is planned, documented and versioned in our private Gitea instance. The documented development record includes 140 commits, 42 tagged releases, 10 architecture decision records and dated changelogs. Every version that reached production was first running in the staging environment: 15 versions went through a production pass; 14 completed and 1 was stopped by a safety check and rolled back automatically.

Code, database changes, data definitions and release documentation are maintained together. A protected main branch, pull requests and automated checks support review and traceability.

Changes follow implementation, staging acceptance checks, approval and production deployment. Production releases use backups, explicit database migrations, file-integrity verification and rollback procedures. Release records distinguish staging versions, production deployments and a deployment stopped and rolled back by a safety check.

Technical verification includes 31 rules-engine checks, 157 automated end-to-end checks across 16 screen sizes and a 119-check infrastructure verification procedure. A four-reviewer security review produced 43 findings tracked with remediation information.

These processes support reliable delivery. They do not replace scientific review, accessibility evaluation or educational testing.

BENEFITS, TEAM CONSIDERATIONS AND EARLY TESTING

The intended benefits are greater familiarity with scientific data, stronger evidence-based reasoning and practice anticipating needs, allocating resources and explaining decisions.

The team considered children’s reading demands, clear visual feedback, accessible interaction, progressively reduced hints, mobile use, privacy and source reliability. The platform works on computers and phones without requiring a child account. Progress remains on the device, and first-party visit analytics (page, browser, referrer and IP address) operate without third-party trackers.

An initial home playtest involved three children ages 7, 9 and 12, who completed the mission and received certificates. This provides preliminary usability feedback, not proof of learning gains. Educator review and structured classroom testing are planned to assess comprehension and application to new situations.

CREATIVITY AND AI USE

Our creative contribution is connecting authentic NASA information, a reusable data architecture and a child-centered learning process. Rather than presenting data only as background material, we use selected records to create questions and choices whose consequences children can explore.

Claude generated and tested much of the code and drafted substantial text. ChatGPT supported artwork generation, with Canva and PowerPoint used for visual preparation. Our team provided the concept, character direction, story and project decisions. AI also supported learning-design planning; human educator review remains a next step.

galaxya.space aims to make NASA’s world of observations and data approachable to children. Its success will ultimately depend on whether they can explain what they observed, understand how information affected the model and apply that understanding to a new challenge.
